lessons.title: Shared keys and the AES block cipher
lessons.summary: AES maps 128-bit blocks under a shared secret key; its key length sets a generic search margin.
lessons.body:
With symmetric encryption, two parties share one secret **key**, and the same key both locks (encrypts) and unlocks (decrypts) the data.

```
 plaintext --[ Enc(key) ]--> ciphertext
ciphertext --[ Dec(key) ]--> plaintext
```

Symmetric encryption is used for bulk data; public-key operations commonly establish or protect its keys. Hardware AES instructions can accelerate it; actual speed depends on the mode, the implementation and the size and pattern of the data.

One principle runs through the whole field. **Kerckhoffs's principle** says a system must stay secure even if the attacker knows everything about it except the key. So the algorithm is public, and all the secrecy lives in the key. "Nobody knows how our cipher works" is not security.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A padlock model anyone can buy
> A well-known padlock model is sold in every hardware shop. Anyone can buy one, take it apart and study the mechanism, yet your particular lock is still safe because only you have its key.
>
> **How it maps:** The published padlock design is the public cipher (AES, its rounds and its mode). The individual key is the secret key. Kerckhoffs's principle says security must survive full knowledge of the design, just as a good padlock model stays useful after its blueprint is public.
>
> **Where it stops:** Physical locks fail to picking, cutting and wear, and a key can be copied from a photograph. A cipher's key cannot be guessed from its design, and the attacker's cost is measured in guesses: each extra key bit doubles the work, which has no padlock equivalent.

> [!warning] Never roll your own
> Everything in this lesson is here so you understand what your library does and can spot misuse. In real code, use a vetted, high-level library (Python's `cryptography`, libsodium, Google Tink, your platform's crypto API). Do not design ciphers, modes or protocols yourself, and do not hand-assemble low-level primitives.

## Block ciphers and AES

A **block cipher** is a keyed permutation on fixed-size blocks. For AES, a given key maps each possible 128-bit input to a unique 128-bit output, and it should look like a random permutation to anyone without the key.

**AES** (the Advanced Encryption Standard, originally Rijndael) is the block cipher you will use:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Block size | 128 bits (16 bytes) |
| Key sizes | 128, 192, 256 bits |
| Rounds | 10, 12, 14 |
| Standard | NIST FIPS 197 (2001) |

AES starts with a round-key addition. Its rounds apply byte substitution, row shifts and round-key addition; all but the final round also mix columns. AES-128 and AES-256 are standardised choices. AES-256 offers a larger key-search margin.

How large is that margin? For an ideal block cipher, generic classical key search tries keys one by one (brute force). This is a baseline work model, not a proof that no cryptanalytic shortcut exists for a concrete algorithm. The relationship to keep in mind is that every extra key bit doubles the number of possible keys:

```formula essential
N_keys = 2^k
where
N_keys: the number of possible keys (the keyspace)
k: the key length in bits: 128, 192 or 256 for AES
In words: each extra key bit doubles the keyspace, so a 129-bit key has twice as many possibilities as a 128-bit key, and a 256-bit key has 2^128 times as many as a 128-bit key.
```

On average a classical search finds the key after trying about half the keyspace. For scale, even an entirely hypothetical trillion guesses per second would need about five billion billion years on average for one uniformly chosen 128-bit key. That is why practical attacks go after how keys are generated, stored and used rather than the key length itself.

Quantum computers change the generic estimate less than many people expect. Grover's algorithm, an idealised quantum search, needs on the order of the square root of the keyspace in queries: about 2^64 for a 128-bit key and about 2^128 for a 256-bit key. That is a query count, not a practical quantum runtime estimate, which is why AES-256 is described as an extra margin rather than a necessity.

One AES block operation processes exactly 16 bytes. Real messages are longer, so you need a **mode of operation** that says how to chain blocks together. The mode is where most real-world mistakes happen.

## Key takeaways
- AES maps 128-bit blocks under a shared secret key; its key length sets a generic search margin.
- Public algorithms and secret keys follow Kerckhoffs’s principle.

## Further reading
- [NIST FIPS 197: AES](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/197/final)
- [Python cryptography: AEAD APIs](https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/aead/)

questions.prompt: A vendor says their product is secure because it uses a secret, in-house encryption algorithm that nobody outside the company has seen. Which principle does this violate?

options.text: Kerckhoffs's principle: a system should stay secure even if everything except the key is public
options.explanation: Correct. Security should rest on the key alone. A secret algorithm can be reverse-engineered from the product, and it has not had public scrutiny.

options.text: The principle of least privilege
options.explanation: Least privilege is about giving each user or process only the access it needs. It isn't about whether an algorithm is public.

options.text: Defence in depth, which forbids relying on one algorithm
options.explanation: Defence in depth means layering controls, but it doesn't say algorithms must be public. The specific principle here is Kerckhoffs's.

options.text: Forward secrecy
options.explanation: Forward secrecy is about past sessions staying safe when long-term keys leak. It says nothing about keeping the algorithm secret.

questions.workedExample:
1. The vendor relies on keeping its algorithm secret.
2. A design should retain its security when the algorithm becomes known and only the key remains secret.
3. Disclosure does not automatically break every private cipher, but secrecy alone is no evidence of robustness.
4. Public scrutiny can expose weaknesses; this prompt supplies no independent evaluation of the private design.

lessons.title: ECB exposes equal plaintext blocks
lessons.summary: Identical AES blocks expose equality under ECB, allowing patterns and block rearrangement.
lessons.body:
## ECB: the mode you must not use

**Electronic Codebook (ECB)** is the obvious approach: split the message into 16-byte blocks and encrypt each independently.

```
P1      P2      P3
|       |       |
AES_k   AES_k   AES_k
|       |       |
C1      C2      C3
```

Each ciphertext block depends only on its own plaintext block and the key. Nothing carries over from one block to the next, and nothing changes between messages.

The problem: **identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks**. Repeated blocks therefore reveal equality directly to an observer. ECB is deterministic per block, so it leaks structure. The famous demonstration encrypts an uncompressed image of the Linux penguin: the "encrypted" image is still clearly a penguin, because every patch of the same colour encrypts to the same bytes.

> [!example] ECB leaks equality
> Encrypt `YELLOW SUBMARINE` twice in a row (32 bytes) with AES-ECB. The two 16-byte ciphertext blocks are byte-for-byte identical. An observer learns "these blocks are equal" without the key.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A phrasebook code
> Imagine a secret code book that turns every common phrase into a fixed code word: "meet at noon" is always "PELICAN". Someone who cannot read the code book still notices when "PELICAN" turns up in three messages, and can copy a code word from one message into another.
>
> **How it maps:** The code book is AES under one key, each phrase is a 16-byte plaintext block, and each code word is a ciphertext block. ECB's name, Electronic Codebook, comes from exactly this idea: same input, same output, every time.
>
> **Where it stops:** ECB works on fixed 16-byte chunks rather than words, so a repeat is only visible when equal data lines up on the same block boundaries. Collecting known plaintext and ciphertext pairs lets an attacker recognise those exact blocks again, but not decrypt new ones: AES itself stays strong, and the leak is equality and rearrangement.

It also lets an attacker cut and paste blocks between messages. If block 3 of one ciphertext encrypts `role=admin;.....`, it can be spliced into another message. Avoid ECB for directly encrypting structured application data; low-level block operations can also be components of correctly designed standard constructions.

## Key takeaways
- ECB repeats ciphertext for identical plaintext blocks under one key.
- Pattern leakage and block rearrangement make ECB unsuitable for structured application data.

## Further reading
- [NIST block cipher modes](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/38/a/final)
- [NIST GCM standard](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/38/d/final)

questions.prompt: A legacy service encrypts customer records with AES in **ECB** mode under one key. Two customers' records both begin with the same 16 bytes, `country=GB;tier=`. What can an eavesdropper who never learns the key tell from the ciphertexts?

options.text: Nothing: AES is secure, so the ciphertexts reveal nothing at all
options.explanation: This confuses the block cipher with the mode. AES itself is strong, but ECB applies it deterministically block by block, so the mode leaks equality.

options.text: That the first block of both records is identical, because ECB encrypts equal blocks to equal ciphertext
options.explanation: Correct. ECB has no IV or chaining, so identical 16-byte plaintext blocks always produce identical ciphertext blocks under the same key.

options.text: The full plaintext of both records, because ECB is reversible without the key
options.explanation: ECB still needs the key to decrypt. Its weakness is leaking patterns and allowing block cut-and-paste, not handing over the plaintext.

options.text: Only the length of the records, which every cipher leaks
options.explanation: Length does leak with most ciphers, but ECB leaks more: which blocks are equal, within and across messages.

questions.workedExample:
ECB splits the data into 16-byte blocks and encrypts each one independently with the same key. Each ciphertext block depends only on its own plaintext block and the key, never on its position or on other blocks.

1. Both records start with the same 16-byte block `country=GB;tier=`.
2. Same key and same input block give the same output, so the first ciphertext blocks match byte for byte.
3. The eavesdropper can't read the block, but learns *these two records share a prefix*. With enough records they can group customers by common values, just like the ECB penguin image.

A mode with a fresh IV or nonce (CBC, CTR, GCM) makes the two ciphertexts look unrelated.

lessons.title: CBC IVs, padding and authentication
lessons.summary: Trace CBC chaining, choose unpredictable IVs and recognise padding-oracle and integrity failures.
lessons.body:
CBC combines each block with the previous ciphertext, using an unpredictable IV to start. Understanding that chain explains why padding errors and unauthenticated changes are dangerous.

## CBC: chaining with an IV

**Cipher Block Chaining (CBC)** XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encrypting. The first block is XORed with an **initialisation vector (IV)**.

**XOR** (exclusive or, written ⊕) is the workhorse of symmetric cryptography. It compares two bit strings position by position:

```formula essential
x ⊕ y ⊕ y = x
where
⊕: XOR (exclusive or): combines two bit strings bit by bit; each output bit is 1 where the inputs differ and 0 where they match
x, y: any two bit strings of the same length, for example two 16-byte blocks
In words: XORing the same value in twice cancels it out, so one operation both applies a mask and removes it. This is why a single XOR can both encrypt and decrypt, and why repeated masks cancel.
```

For example, the bytes 0x31 (`0011 0001`) and 0x37 (`0011 0111`) XOR to 0x06 (`0000 0110`): only the two positions that differ come out as 1.

```
IV --XOR      +----XOR      +----XOR
     |        |     |       |     |
     P1       |     P2      |     P3
     |        |     |       |     |
   AES_k      |   AES_k     |   AES_k
     |        |     |       |     |
     C1 ------+     C2 -----+     C3
```

Put simply: before encryption, each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block (the IV for the first block). Decryption runs AES backwards on a block and then XORs the previous ciphertext block back out. That last step matters later: whatever an attacker does to one ciphertext block lands, bit for bit, in the next decrypted plaintext block (and scrambles the block it sits in).

```formula reference
C_0 = IV
C_i = E_k(P_i ⊕ C_{i−1})
P_i = D_k(C_i) ⊕ C_{i−1}
where
C_i: the i-th ciphertext block, 16 bytes
C_{i−1}: the ciphertext block just before it
C_0: the starting value, set to the IV
IV: the initialisation vector, a random 16-byte block sent along with the ciphertext
P_i: the i-th plaintext block, 16 bytes
i: the block number, counting from 1
E_k: one AES block encryption under the secret key k
D_k: one AES block decryption under k, which undoes E_k
k: the secret key
⊕: XOR (exclusive or): each output bit is 1 where the two inputs differ and 0 where they match
In words: encryption mixes each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before AES; decryption undoes AES and then XORs the previous ciphertext block back out, so a change to one ciphertext block flips the same bits in the next plaintext block.
```

If the first two plaintext blocks are both `YELLOW SUBMARINE`, each is mixed with a different chaining value in the usual case. Repeated plaintext no longer forces repeated ciphertext, although accidental block equality remains possible. Use a fresh **random and unpredictable** IV for each CBC message; also authenticate it with the ciphertext. This prevents the deterministic equality pattern of ECB under the scheme’s assumptions. A predictable IV broke TLS 1.0 (the BEAST attack, 2011).

CBC has two big weaknesses:

- **Padding.** Messages must be padded to a multiple of 16 bytes (usually PKCS#7). If a server reveals whether the padding was valid, through an error message or even response timing, an attacker can decrypt the whole message one byte at a time. These are **padding oracle** attacks; Lucky Thirteen and POODLE exploit particular TLS/SSL CBC constructions and observable differences. Exploitation depends on obtaining a usable oracle and enough queries.
- **No integrity.** CBC hides the content but does not stop tampering.

PKCS#7 padding always adds between 1 and 16 bytes, and every padding byte holds the number of bytes added, so the receiver knows how many to strip. A message that already fills whole blocks gets a whole extra block of sixteen `0x10` bytes, so the last byte can always be read as a count. A 10-byte message gets six bytes of `0x06`. A padding oracle works by tweaking the previous ciphertext block until the server says the last byte decrypted to a valid padding value such as `0x01`.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A clerk with two rejection stamps
> A clerk checks sealed forms you cannot read. Forms with a badly filled-in last box get stamped "bad ending"; everything else that fails gets "rejected". By submitting many slightly altered copies and watching which stamp comes back, you can work out what was written in the last box, one character at a time.
>
> **How it maps:** The clerk is the server decrypting CBC; the "bad ending" stamp is a distinguishable padding error (an error message, status code or timing difference). Each altered copy is a ciphertext whose previous block the attacker has tweaked, and each answer reveals whether the decrypted last byte formed valid padding.
>
> **Where it stops:** A real clerk's answer would not let you calculate hidden text. The attack works because CBC decryption XORs the previous ciphertext block into the plaintext, so the attacker's tweak and the padding rule together pin down each byte exactly. Without that XOR structure, two stamps would leak far less.

## Key takeaways
- CBC uses an unpredictable IV, block chaining and unambiguous padding.
- CBC alone lacks integrity; observable padding differences can become an attack oracle.

## Further reading
- [NIST block cipher modes](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/38/a/final)
- [NIST GCM standard](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/38/d/final)

questions.prompt: You encrypt messages with AES-CBC using a random IV each time, but no MAC. Which property are you still missing?

options.text: Confidentiality: CBC doesn't hide the content
options.explanation: CBC with a random IV does provide confidentiality against passive attackers. What it lacks is protection against changes.

options.text: Availability: CBC messages can be lost
options.explanation: Availability needs system-level measures. The possibility of losing messages is not the missing cryptographic authentication guarantee described here.

options.text: Integrity: an attacker can modify the ciphertext and you won't detect it
options.explanation: Correct. Without a MAC, flipped bits decrypt to altered plaintext (or a padding error that becomes an oracle). An AEAD like AES-GCM adds the missing tag.

options.text: Key secrecy: CBC leaks the key through the IV
options.explanation: The IV is public by design and reveals nothing about the key. The missing property is integrity.

questions.workedExample:
CBC decryption runs AES backwards on each ciphertext block and then XORs the *previous* ciphertext block into the result. An attacker in transit can change any ciphertext byte.

1. Encryption alone answers "can an attacker read it?" Properly used CBC with unpredictable IVs is intended to protect against passive observers.
2. It does not answer "can an attacker change it?" Flipping a bit of the first ciphertext block flips exactly the same bit of the second plaintext block (and scrambles the first, which passes through AES decryption). Nothing in CBC notices.
3. Worse, if your server reacts differently to bad padding, the attacker gets a padding oracle and may recover plaintext through repeated adaptive queries.
4. The fix is authenticated encryption: AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, whose safe API rejects failed authentication before returning plaintext.

questions.prompt: Your API decrypts AES-CBC tokens. On a bad token it returns HTTP 400 with `invalid padding` or HTTP 401 with `invalid token`, depending on where decoding failed. A pentester says they can decrypt any token. What is the best fix?

options.text: Make both errors return the same message and status code
options.explanation: That narrows the leak but timing differences can still reveal the padding result, as Lucky Thirteen showed. It treats the symptom of an unauthenticated design.

options.text: Switch to a random IV for every token
options.explanation: A random IV is already needed for CBC confidentiality but does nothing against a padding oracle, which works on any IV.

options.text: Use AES-256 instead of AES-128
options.explanation: Key length is irrelevant: the attack never touches the key. It exploits the server's padding feedback.

options.text: Replace the scheme with a vetted AEAD API such as AESGCM, and reject authentication failures without processing plaintext
options.explanation: Correct. AESGCM needs no CBC padding, and its high-level decrypt API raises an error instead of returning unauthenticated plaintext.

questions.workedExample:
1. The two error responses tell the attacker whether a modified token's padding was valid. That yes/no answer is a padding oracle.
2. CBC decryption XORs the previous ciphertext block into each decrypted block, so by tweaking that previous block and watching the answers, the attacker can work out the plaintext one byte at a time without the key.
3. The attack needs many adaptive requests; how many depends on the oracle's reliability and noise, but it is well within reach of an automated tool.
4. Making the two errors identical narrows the leak, but timing differences can still reveal the padding result, as Lucky Thirteen showed.
5. The robust fix removes the oracle's cause: use a vetted AEAD such as AESGCM, whose decrypt call verifies the tag and raises an error instead of returning unauthenticated plaintext, and never act on output that failed verification.

lessons.title: CTR counters and repeated keystreams
lessons.summary: CTR XORs a counter-derived keystream with data and must never repeat counter blocks under one key.
lessons.body:
## CTR: turning a block cipher into a stream cipher

**Counter mode (CTR)** encrypts a counter, `nonce || 0`, `nonce || 1`, `nonce || 2`... to produce a **keystream**, then XORs the keystream with the plaintext.

```
nonce||0  nonce||1  nonce||2
   |         |         |
 AES_k     AES_k     AES_k
   |         |         |
  K1        K2        K3   keystream
   XOR P1    XOR P2    XOR P3
   =C1       =C2       =C3
```

AES never touches the message itself. It only encrypts the counter blocks, and the output (the keystream) is XORed with the plaintext. Decryption regenerates the same keystream from the key, nonce and counter and XORs it off again.

```formula reference
K_i = E_k(N ‖ i)
C_i = P_i ⊕ K_i
where
K_i: the i-th 16-byte keystream block (K1, K2, … in the diagram)
E_k: one AES block encryption under the secret key k
k: the secret key
N: the nonce, a value used only once per key (96 bits in GCM)
i: the block counter: 0, 1, 2, … (GCM starts its data blocks at 2)
‖: concatenation: the bits of N followed by the bits of i, filling one 16-byte counter block
C_i: the i-th ciphertext block
P_i: the i-th plaintext block (the last block may be shorter; the extra keystream is thrown away)
⊕: XOR (exclusive or): each output bit is 1 where the two inputs differ and 0 where they match
In words: the keystream depends only on the key, the nonce and the block number, never on the message, so the same key and nonce always produce the same keystream.
```

CTR needs no padding, blocks can be processed in parallel, and you can decrypt from the middle. But it has one absolute rule: **never repeat a counter block with the same key**. Use non-overlapping nonce/counter ranges, and prevent counter wraparound.

## What goes wrong when a keystream repeats

Because the keystream ignores the message, reusing a key and nonce gives two messages the *same* keystream. An eavesdropper who XORs the two ciphertexts together makes that shared keystream cancel:

```formula essential
C_1 ⊕ C_2 = P_1 ⊕ P_2
where
C_1, C_2: two ciphertexts encrypted under the same key and nonce, which the attacker can see
P_1, P_2: the two plaintexts
⊕: XOR (exclusive or): each output bit is 1 where the two inputs differ and 0 where they match
In words: the shared keystream appears in both ciphertexts and cancels, so the attacker gets the XOR of the two plaintexts without ever touching the key.
```

That alone is not both messages, but real messages are rarely random. Wherever the attacker knows or can guess one plaintext (a fixed JSON header, an HTTP request line, a file signature), XORing it into the result reveals the other message's bytes at the same positions. Guesses for one message can be checked against the other until both read sensibly. This repeated-keystream failure is called the "two-time pad".

Typical ways it happens in real systems:

- a nonce hard-coded as all zeros "for now";
- a counter stored in memory that restarts at zero after a reboot or redeploy;
- several servers or devices sharing one key, each starting its own counter at zero;
- a random nonce that is too short for the number of messages, so repeats become likely.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: The same noise track under two recordings
> Imagine two private phone calls, each disguised by mixing in an identical recorded noise track. Line the two disguised recordings up and subtract one from the other: the noise cancels exactly, and what remains is the difference between the two conversations. If you know what was said in one call, you can recover the other.
>
> **How it maps:** The noise track is the keystream, each call is a plaintext, and subtracting recordings is XORing ciphertexts. Using the same noise track twice is reusing a key and nonce.
>
> **Where it stops:** Audio subtraction is approximate, while XOR cancellation is exact for every bit. And the leftover is not a muddled mix you can hear through: it is the bitwise XOR of the plaintexts, which needs known or guessed text from one message before the other becomes readable.

## Key takeaways
- CTR XORs a counter-derived keystream with data and must never repeat counter blocks under one key.
- Reusing a key and nonce makes the keystream cancel, exposing the XOR of the plaintexts; known or guessed text then reveals the other message.

## Further reading
- [NIST SP 800-38A: block cipher modes](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/38/a/final)
- [NIST SP 800-38D: GCM](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/38/d/final)

questions.prompt: A sensor fleet encrypts readings with AES-CTR. Every device shares one key, and each starts its nonce and counter at zero after a reboot. Every message begins with the same 24-byte header, `{"type":"reading","v":2,`, followed by the reading. An eavesdropper captures messages from two devices that both just rebooted. What can they learn without the key?

options.text: Nothing: without the key, CTR ciphertext reveals nothing
options.explanation: That holds only while every key and counter block is used once. Here both devices produced the same keystream, which cancels when the two ciphertexts are XORed.

options.text: The AES key, by XORing the two ciphertexts
options.explanation: XORing the ciphertexts removes the keystream; it does not reveal the key. AES itself is not attacked.

options.text: The XOR of the two readings, and any reading bytes whose counterpart in the other message they know or can guess
options.explanation: Correct. The shared keystream cancels, leaving the XOR of the plaintexts. The identical headers XOR to zero and reveal nothing new, but a known or guessed byte in one reading exposes the byte at the same position in the other.

options.text: Only the message lengths, which every cipher leaks
options.explanation: Lengths do leak, but keystream reuse leaks much more: the XOR of the plaintexts, from which known or guessed content reveals the other message.

questions.workedExample:
1. CTR's keystream depends only on the key, nonce and counter, never on the message.
2. Same key, both devices restarting at nonce and counter zero: both messages are XORed with the *same* keystream. This is a two-time pad.
3. XORing the two ciphertexts cancels that keystream and leaves the XOR of the two plaintexts.
4. The identical headers cancel to zero bytes, which confirms the reuse but reveals nothing new. The readings differ, so their XOR is a relationship between them.
5. Any byte the attacker knows or can guess in one reading (a typical value, a field name, a unit) reveals the matching byte of the other. With many rebooted devices the attacker gets many such pairs.
6. Fixes: per-device keys and nonces that never repeat across reboots (a persisted counter, or random nonces long enough for the message volume). Moving to an AEAD such as AES-GCM adds authentication but keeps exactly the same nonce rule, so the nonce fix is still required.

lessons.title: How unauthenticated ciphertext can change
lessons.summary: CTR ciphertext bit changes become the same plaintext bit changes.
lessons.body:
CTR decryption removes its keystream with XOR. That reversibility also lets an active attacker apply chosen differences without learning the key.

## The missing piece: integrity

Properly used encryption can provide **confidentiality** against its intended attacker model; unauthenticated modes can fail under active attacks. It does not give **integrity**: an attacker may still change it. With CTR (or any stream cipher), flipping a bit in the ciphertext flips exactly that bit in the plaintext.

> [!example] Malleability in practice
> A server encrypts `pay Bob 10` with AES-CTR. The attacker doesn't know the key but guesses the format. They XOR byte 8 of the ciphertext with `'1' XOR '9'` (that's `0x08`). The server decrypts `pay Bob 90` without complaint.

Why it works: decryption just XORs the keystream back off, so any difference the attacker XORs into a ciphertext byte passes straight through into the decrypted byte. The keystream cancels as usual and the attacker's change survives, so a guessed plaintext byte can be turned into any byte they like.

In the example, the difference is the XOR of the characters `1` and `9` (`0x31` and `0x39`), which is `0x08`. The attacker needs only two things: a guess at the plaintext in that position (message formats are rarely secret) and the ability to change data in transit or in storage. They never need the key.

The same weakness affects CBC in a block-shaped form: flipping bits in one ciphertext block flips the same bits in the next plaintext block. Adding more encryption does not help. What is missing is a check that the ciphertext is exactly what the sender produced.

The lesson: **unauthenticated encryption is almost never what you want**. You need a way to detect any change before you act on decrypted data.

## Key takeaways
- CTR ciphertext bit changes become the same plaintext bit changes.
- Confidentiality alone does not provide integrity; authenticate before using decrypted data.

## Further reading
- [NIST SP 800-38A: block cipher modes](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/38/a/final)
- [Python cryptography: AEAD APIs](https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/aead/)

questions.prompt: A payments service encrypts `amount=100` with AES-CTR and no MAC, and an attacker on the network wants the server to decrypt `amount=700` instead. Which of these does the attacker actually need?

options.text: The AES key, so they can decrypt, edit and re-encrypt the message
options.explanation: Unauthenticated CTR is malleable: decryption carries flipped ciphertext bits straight into the plaintext, so no key is required.

options.text: The nonce, because it must be secret for CTR to be secure
options.explanation: The nonce is public and only has to be unique. It plays no part in this attack.

options.text: To know or guess the byte at that position (`1`) and to be able to change the ciphertext in transit
options.explanation: Correct. XORing the difference between `1` and `7` into the ciphertext byte at that position changes the decrypted `1` into `7`. Only the guessed plaintext and the ability to modify data are needed.

options.text: Many captured messages under the same nonce, so the keystream cancels
options.explanation: That describes the two-time pad, a separate failure. Malleability works on a single message with a correctly unique nonce.

questions.workedExample:
1. CTR decryption XORs each ciphertext byte with a keystream byte. Whatever difference the attacker XORs into a ciphertext byte appears, unchanged, in the decrypted byte.
2. The attacker guesses the format, so they know which byte holds `1`.
3. They XOR that ciphertext byte with the difference between `1` (0x31) and `7` (0x37), which is 0x06. The server decrypts `amount=700`.
4. They never learn the key or the keystream, and the nonce is irrelevant.
5. Defence: authenticated encryption. With AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 the changed ciphertext fails tag verification and decryption raises an error instead of returning `amount=700`.

lessons.title: Authenticated encryption through a library
lessons.summary: AEAD encrypts data and authenticates it together with optional public associated data.
lessons.body:
## AEAD: what you should actually use

**Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD)** does both jobs in one primitive. It encrypts the plaintext and computes an authentication **tag** over the ciphertext plus optional **associated data** (headers that must not be changed but needn't be secret, such as a record ID or protocol version). A safe API returns plaintext only after successful authentication. Internal decryption may happen before verification; callers must not use unauthenticated output.

Two common AEAD configurations (GCM also defines other permitted tag lengths):

| AEAD | Nonce | Tag | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| AES-256-GCM | 96 bits | 128 bits | Fast with AES-NI |
| ChaCha20-Poly1305 | 96 bits | 128 bits | Fast in software |

**AES-GCM** combines CTR encryption with a tag formed from the GHASH polynomial authentication function and a nonce-dependent AES mask. GHASH alone is not a secure standalone MAC. **ChaCha20-Poly1305** (RFC 8439) pairs a stream cipher with the Poly1305 MAC; it is quick on phones and devices without AES instructions. TLS 1.3 only allows AEAD cipher suites, and these two are the common choices.

Here is what it looks like with Python's `cryptography` library:

```python
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives \
    .ciphers.aead import AESGCM

# Generate a fresh random AES key.
key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)
aead = AESGCM(key)

# A random demo nonce; never reuse per key.
nonce = os.urandom(12)  # random
aad = b"order-id:4711"  # authed, not secret
# AAD is authenticated without encryption.
ct = aead.encrypt(nonce, b"pay Bob 10", aad)

print(len(ct))           # 10 + 16-byte tag
# Release plaintext only after a valid tag.
print(aead.decrypt(nonce, ct, aad))
```

This prints `26` and then `b'pay Bob 10'`. GCM adds no padding: the output is the 10-byte ciphertext with a 16-byte (128-bit) tag appended. The 12-byte nonce is not part of that output.

An invalid tag makes `decrypt` raise `InvalidTag` instead of returning plaintext. Altering `ct`, the nonce or `aad` is intended to fail authentication under the scheme’s forgery bounds; the probability of an accepted forgery is small, not mathematically zero. You store or send the nonce alongside the ciphertext; it doesn't need to be secret, only unique.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A parcel with tamper-evident tape over the label
> A courier parcel is sealed with tamper-evident tape that also runs over the address label. Anyone can read the label, but if the contents or the label are disturbed the tape shows it, and the recipient refuses the parcel unopened.
>
> **How it maps:** The sealed contents are the ciphertext; the readable label under the tape is the associated data, authenticated but not secret; the tape is the authentication tag. A safe AEAD API is the recipient who refuses the parcel: `decrypt` raises `InvalidTag` and hands back nothing.
>
> **Where it stops:** A skilled forger can sometimes reseal a parcel; an AEAD forgery has a tiny, bounded probability instead. And there is no parcel equivalent of the nonce rule: reusing a nonce under one key can quietly destroy both secrecy and the tag's protection.

Python `cryptography`'s **Fernet** manages a random IV and token format for authenticated encryption, but has no associated-data interface. Libsodium's low-level `secretbox` requires the caller to supply a nonce; some wrappers manage it. Check the specific API rather than assuming automatic nonce generation.

## Key takeaways
- AEAD encrypts data and authenticates it together with optional public associated data.
- The demonstrated AESGCM API appends a 16-byte tag and rejects failed authentication.

## Further reading
- [Python cryptography: AEAD APIs](https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/aead/)
- [NIST SP 800-38D: GCM](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/38/d/final)

questions.prompt: Which statements about Python cryptography AESGCM with a 128-bit tag are true? Output means its encrypt() result, excluding separately stored nonce and AAD. Select all that apply.

options.text: The nonce must never repeat under the same key
options.explanation: Correct. Repetition reuses the CTR keystream and can enable authentication-key attacks and forgeries.

options.text: Associated data (AAD) is encrypted along with the plaintext
options.explanation: AAD is authenticated but not encrypted by this operation; it need not be transmitted if both parties already know it.

options.text: A failed authentication check raises an error and returns no plaintext
options.explanation: Correct. AESGCM.decrypt raises InvalidTag when its tag verification fails. Protection has a bounded nonzero forgery probability, rather than a mathematical guarantee that every possible altered input is rejected.

options.text: The nonce must be kept secret like the key
options.explanation: The nonce only has to be unique. It is usually stored or sent alongside the ciphertext in plain view.

options.text: The output is 16 bytes longer than the plaintext
options.explanation: Correct. GCM adds no padding; the ciphertext is the same length as the plaintext plus a 16-byte tag.

questions.workedExample:
Go through each claim against how GCM is built (CTR encryption plus a GHASH tag):

1. Nonce uniqueness: CTR keystream depends on key and nonce, so repeating it repeats the keystream. **True.**
2. AAD: it feeds into the tag only. **False**: it's authenticated, not secret.
3. Tampering: decryption recomputes the tag; any mismatch raises `InvalidTag`. **True.**
4. Nonce secrecy: not required, it travels with the message. **False.**
5. Length: GCM adds no padding, so `encrypt()` returns exactly the plaintext length plus the 16-byte tag (a 10-byte message gives 26 bytes). **True.**

questions.prompt:
A developer stores AES-GCM records like this, then reports that every decryption fails with `InvalidTag`:

```python
def save(key, data):
    n = os.urandom(12)
    ct = AESGCM(key).encrypt(
        n, data, None)
    return ct  # stored in the DB

def load(key, ct):
    n = os.urandom(12)
    return AESGCM(key).decrypt(
        n, ct, None)
```

What is wrong, and what is the fix?

options.text: AES-GCM cannot decrypt data in a different process; keep records in memory
options.explanation: GCM works across processes and machines. The failure comes from the inputs given to decrypt, not where it runs.

options.text: The key is wrong; generate a new key in `load` as well
options.explanation: A different key would also fail. Encryption and decryption must use the same key, and the same nonce.

options.text: Decryption uses a fresh random nonce instead of the one used to encrypt; store the 12-byte nonce with each ciphertext (for example, prepended) and pass it back to decrypt
options.explanation: Correct. The nonce must match. It is not secret, only unique per key, so storing it next to the ciphertext is standard practice.

options.text: `InvalidTag` means the data was tampered with; restore the database from backup
options.explanation: InvalidTag means verification failed, which tampering would cause, but here the code itself supplies the wrong nonce for every record.

questions.workedExample:
1. GCM derives its keystream and its tag mask from the key and the nonce. Decryption must use the same key, nonce and associated data that encryption used.
2. `load` invents a new random nonce, so the recomputed tag can never match. The safe API raises `InvalidTag` rather than returning garbage plaintext, which is exactly what you want.
3. The nonce does not need to be secret, only never reused under the same key. Store it with the record, for example `n + ct`, and split off the first 12 bytes in `load`.
4. Do not "fix" this by using a fixed nonce for every record: that would make decryption work while reusing the nonce under one key, which breaks GCM's confidentiality and authentication.

lessons.title: Nonce discipline and GCM usage limits
lessons.summary: A GCM nonce repeat can leak plaintext relations and enable authentication forgeries.
lessons.body:
## GCM's sharp edge: nonce reuse

GCM inherits CTR's nonce rule, and the consequences are worse. Reusing a nonce under the same key:

1. Leaks `P1 XOR P2`, exactly as in CTR.
2. Can expose equations for GCM's authentication key and enable **forgeries**. Distinct messages, tag length and available observations affect whether the key is uniquely recovered.

Random nonces can collide by chance, and the chance grows with the *square* of the number of messages, because every pair of messages is a chance for a match (the birthday effect, covered properly in the hashing units later in this module). For 96-bit random nonces the risk is negligible for a few billion messages under one key, but it would approach a coin flip around 2^48 messages, which busy services can reach.

```formula reference
p_coll ≈ q^2 / 2^(b+1)
where
p_coll: the probability that at least two of the q messages got the same nonce, from 0 (never) to 1 (certain)
q: the number of messages encrypted under one key
b: the nonce length in bits, 96 for standard GCM
2^(b+1): twice the number of possible nonces, 2^b; the factor 2 comes from counting each pair of messages once
≈: approximately equal to; the approximation is good while p_coll is small
In words: the chance of a random-nonce repeat grows with the square of the message count, so at 2^32 messages it is about 2^−33 (roughly 1 in 8.6 billion) for 96-bit nonces.
```

NIST SP 800-38D requires the chance that one key is ever used with a repeated IV on different data to be at most 2^−32, and for random 96-bit nonces it caps each key at 2^32 (about 4.3 billion) encryptions. At that cap the collision chance is about 1 in 8.6 billion, inside the requirement. Apply the limit across all devices using that key, plus message-length and tag-dependent limits. These figures come from the 2007 standard; NIST is revising it, but as of October 2026 it had published only calls for comments (proposing, among other things, to drop tags shorter than 96 bits), not a revised draft. A counter requires coordinated uniqueness across restarts and workers. **AES-GCM-SIV** tolerates accidental nonce repetition better, though repetition can still leak equality and usage limits remain. **XChaCha20-Poly1305** has a 192-bit nonce that makes random collisions negligible at practical volumes; it is **not** nonce-misuse resistant and must not repeat a nonce under a key.

## Common mistakes

- **ECB for application data.** Select the intended authenticated scheme explicitly.
- **Hard-coded or reused IVs and nonces**, such as a zero IV "for simplicity".
- **Encryption without authentication**, such as AES-CBC with no MAC, which invites padding oracles and tampering.
- **Using a password as the key.** Keys must be random bytes; derive a key from a password with a password KDF (covered later in password hashing).
- **Ignoring decryption failures** or showing different errors for "bad padding" and "bad MAC", which builds an oracle.
- **Keys in source code.** Use a key management service or secrets manager.

## Key takeaways
- A GCM nonce repeat can leak plaintext relations and enable authentication forgeries.
- Coordinate nonce uniqueness, key rotation and usage limits across all workers and restarts.

## Further reading
- [NIST SP 800-38D: GCM](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/38/d/final)
- [Python cryptography: AEAD APIs](https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/aead/)

questions.prompt: A telemetry pipeline encrypts about 20 million small messages per day per key with AES-GCM, using a random 96-bit nonce each time. It never rotates keys. NIST SP 800-38D caps random-nonce GCM at about 4.3 billion (2^32) encryptions per key, across every instance using that key. A reviewer flags a problem. What is it, and what is the best fix?

options.text: 96-bit nonces are too short to be random, so each one must be a timestamp
options.explanation: Timestamps can repeat (clock skew, parallel workers). The issue is the total number of random nonces per key, not randomness itself.

options.text: After roughly 215 days it exceeds the random-IV invocation limit; rotate keys and manage nonce uniqueness across the deployment
options.explanation: Correct. 4.3 billion encryptions at twenty million a day is reached after roughly 215 days. Collision risk grows continuously with the message count; the cap is where NIST's risk budget runs out, not a cliff edge. A deterministic counter needs coordinated uniqueness and still has other usage limits.

options.text: GCM can't encrypt small messages securely; use CBC instead
options.explanation: Message size isn't the issue, and CBC brings back padding oracles and no integrity.

options.text: The tag is only 128 bits, so it should be lengthened to 256 bits
options.explanation: GCM's tag is at most 128 bits, which is plenty. The risk is nonce reuse.

questions.workedExample:
1. Random 96-bit nonces can collide by chance, and the risk grows with the square of the number of messages under one key. NIST keeps that risk tiny by capping random-nonce GCM at 2^32 (about 4.3 billion) encryptions per key, counted across every server or device sharing the key.
2. At 20 million messages a day, 4.3 billion is reached in about 215 days, roughly seven months. A key that is never rotated will pass the cap, and the collision risk keeps climbing afterwards.
3. A single repeated nonce leaks the XOR of the two plaintexts and may let an attacker recover the GHASH key and forge messages.
4. Fixes: rotate keys well before the cap; or use a coordinated per-key counter that cannot repeat across restarts or workers; or use XChaCha20-Poly1305 (192-bit random nonces, still never reuse one) or AES-GCM-SIV (more tolerant of accidental repeats, with its own limits).

questions.prompt: An IoT firmware bug repeats a GCM nonce under one key for distinct messages. Which information is revealed or attacks can become possible? Select all that apply.

options.text: The XOR of the two plaintexts is revealed
options.explanation: Correct. GCM encrypts with CTR mode, so the same keystream is applied to both messages and cancels out when the two ciphertexts are XORed together.

options.text: The attacker may recover GHASH-key candidates and forge valid tags
options.explanation: Correct. Repeated-nonce tag equations can constrain H, the GHASH authentication key. Whether they uniquely recover it depends on the messages, tag length and observations; the integrity risk is severe.

options.text: The AES key itself is directly recovered
options.explanation: Nonce reuse does not directly recover the AES key. It exposes repeated keystream relationships and may reveal the derived GHASH key.

options.text: Nothing happens as long as the messages are different
options.explanation: Repeating a nonce violates the scheme's rule. Even matching plaintexts need not mean identical authenticated inputs: different AAD can provide additional tag equations. Distinct plaintexts expose their overlapping XOR.

options.text: Other messages encrypted under different nonces become decryptable
options.explanation: Their keystreams are different, so they don't leak directly. But forged messages could now be injected, so you should rotate the key.

questions.workedExample:
GCM encrypts with CTR mode, so a repeated nonce means a repeated keystream. XORing the two ciphertexts cancels it and leaves the XOR of the two plaintexts for anyone who sees both.

1. This reveals a relationship over the overlapping length, not necessarily both plaintexts.
2. With full tags, XORing repeated-nonce tag equations cancels their common mask and gives an equation in H, the GHASH authentication key (derived from the AES key). It may have multiple candidates; identical authenticated inputs add no new equation.
3. Suitable observations can let the attacker pin down H and forge tags. Knowing H and one valid record also exposes that nonce's tag mask.
4. This does not directly recover the AES key or decrypt records under other nonces.
5. Replace the compromised key and fix nonce allocation; using AES-GCM-SIV still requires observing its limits.

questions.prompt:
A developer writes:

```python
key = hashlib.sha256(
    user_password.encode()
).digest()
aead = AESGCM(key)
```

The 32-byte key has the right length for AES-256. What is the main weakness?

options.text: SHA-256 output isn't random enough to be an AES key
options.explanation: A 32-byte hash has the right format, but hashing a small password candidate set does not create a uniform secret chosen from all 2^256 keys.

options.text: The key is too long; AESGCM needs 16 bytes
options.explanation: AESGCM accepts 16, 24 or 32-byte keys, so 32 bytes is valid.

options.text: A hash isn't reversible, so decryption will fail
options.explanation: Decryption uses the same derived key, so it works. The issue is attackers deriving it too.

options.text: Its strength is limited by the password, and plain SHA-256 adds little cost to offline password guessing
options.explanation: Correct. Use a salted, slow, memory-hard password KDF such as Argon2id or scrypt to derive the key, or better, a random key protected by a key-management service.

questions.workedExample:
1. Hashing is deterministic, so it cannot add any secrecy that the password did not have: the key is exactly as guessable as the password.
2. How guessable that is depends on how the password was chosen; human-chosen passwords are often in attackers' candidate lists.
3. Anyone holding a nonce, ciphertext and tag can test a candidate offline: hash it, try AESGCM decryption, and see whether the tag verifies. No rate limit applies offline.
4. Plain SHA-256 is designed to be fast, so each of those offline guesses is cheap; attackers can test enormous candidate lists on their own hardware.
5. Fix: derive the key with a salted, deliberately slow, memory-hard password KDF such as Argon2id or scrypt, storing the salt and parameters, or better, use a random key held in a key-management service.

lessons.title: Digests and three different security goals
lessons.summary: A hash is deterministic and keyless; it does not encrypt its input.
lessons.body:
A **cryptographic hash function** takes a message within its defined length limits and produces a short, fixed-size **digest** (also called a hash or fingerprint). SHA-256 always outputs 256 bits, whether you feed it one byte or a 4 GB disk image.

```
"abc"      --SHA-256--> ba7816bf...f20015ad
"abd"      --SHA-256--> a52d159f...298449c9
4 GB file  --SHA-256--> (another 32 bytes)
```

There is no key. Anyone can compute the hash of anything, and the same input always gives the same output. That makes a hash a public, deterministic fingerprint: a matching digest is useful evidence under the hash's security assumptions, not proof that two inputs must be identical.

Notice that changing one letter (`c` to `d`) changed the whole digest. This is the **avalanche effect**: flipping any input bit should flip about half the output bits, unpredictably.

> [!warning] A hash is not encryption
> There is no key and no way back. You cannot "decrypt" a hash. People who say "we hash the data so it's encrypted" are usually confused, and if the input has low entropy (a phone number, a password) an attacker can simply hash every candidate and compare.

## The three security properties

A function that just compresses data (like CRC32) is not enough. A cryptographic hash must resist three kinds of attack. To compare them, count an attacker's work as the number of hash computations a generic attack needs against an ideal hash with an n-bit digest. The key relationship is that finding *any* clash is far cheaper than hitting a *particular* digest:

```formula essential
W_pre ≈ 2^n
W_coll ≈ 2^(n/2)
where
W_pre: the work to find a preimage (or a second preimage): an input that matches one particular digest, counted in hash computations
W_coll: the work to find a collision: any two different inputs with equal digests
n: the digest length in bits: 256 for SHA-256, 160 for SHA-1, 128 for MD5
≈: approximately equal to
In words: hitting one particular digest takes about 2^n tries, but finding any two inputs that clash takes only about 2^(n/2), its square root. For SHA-256 that is about 2^256 versus 2^128.
```

These are generic classical work estimates for an ideal hash and suitably unconstrained inputs, not guarantees for weak input dictionaries or every long-message construction. The square root comes from the birthday effect, explained in the next unit.

| Property | Attacker's task | Ideal cost |
|---|---|---|
| Preimage | Given a digest, find any input that hashes to it | Full digest-space scale |
| Second preimage | Given one input, find a different input with the same hash | Full digest-space scale |
| Collision | Find any two different inputs with equal hashes | Square-root digest-space scale |

**Preimage resistance** (one-wayness) means you can't run the hash backwards. **Second-preimage resistance** means that, given a specific document, you can't craft a different one with the same fingerprint. **Collision resistance** means you can't find *any* two inputs that clash, even ones you choose freely.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Fingerprints
> Police can match a fingerprint to a suspect on file, but a fingerprint alone does not let them reconstruct the person. Fingerprints are meant to be practically unique, even though nothing in principle stops two people sharing one.
>
> **How it maps:** The person is the input and the fingerprint is the digest. A preimage attack is building a person to fit a given print; a second-preimage attack is finding someone whose print matches a particular suspect's; a collision attack is finding *any* two people in the world with matching prints, which is far easier to stumble on.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real fingerprints were never designed against an adversary, and only the owner can produce theirs. Anyone can compute a digest of any input, there is no key, and the hash's resistance is a calculated work estimate rather than a biological accident.

Collisions must exist: there are more permitted messages than the 2^256 possible SHA-256 outputs. The point is that nobody should be able to *find* one.

Collision search has the lower generic work bound for a fixed digest size. These are distinct security notions with precise assumptions; finding some colliding pair does not let an attacker replace any chosen existing document.

## Key takeaways
- A hash is deterministic and keyless; it does not encrypt its input.
- Preimage, second-preimage and collision resistance describe distinct attacker tasks.

## Further reading
- [NIST FIPS 180-4: secure hashes](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final)
- [NIST FIPS 202: SHA-3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/202/final)
- [Python hashlib API](https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html)

questions.prompt: Two servers on different continents each compute `hashlib.sha256(b"invoice-4711").hexdigest()`. What can you say about the results?

options.text: They differ, because each server uses a random salt
options.explanation: Plain SHA-256 has no salt or key. Salts are something *you* add, for example in password hashing.

options.text: They are identical, because a hash is deterministic and keyless
options.explanation: Correct. The same input always gives the same 64-hex-character digest on any machine. That's what makes hashes usable as fingerprints.

options.text: They differ in the last few characters due to floating-point rounding
options.explanation: Hashes work on bits with integer operations; there is no floating point and no rounding.

options.text: They are identical only if both servers share a secret key
options.explanation: There is no key in SHA-256. A keyed checksum is a MAC, covered in the next lesson.

questions.workedExample:
A cryptographic hash is a fixed, public function of its input alone: no key, no salt, no clock, no machine-specific state.

1. So the same input always gives the same digest.
2. The SHA-256 algorithm is specified bit for bit in FIPS 180-4, so every correct implementation agrees.
3. Both servers therefore compute exactly the same 32 bytes (64 hex characters).
4. Change a single character of the input (`4712`) and, thanks to the avalanche effect, about half the output bits change.

questions.prompt: In 2017 researchers published two different PDF files with the same SHA-1 digest. Which property did this break?

options.text: Collision resistance
options.explanation: Correct. They found a pair of distinct inputs with equal hashes, where they controlled both inputs. That is exactly a collision.

options.text: Preimage resistance
options.explanation: A preimage attack would start from a given digest and find any input for it. SHAttered didn't start from an existing digest.

options.text: Determinism
options.explanation: SHA-1 is still deterministic; each PDF always hashes to the same value. The problem is that two different files share it.

options.text: The avalanche effect
options.explanation: SHA-1 still scrambles its output thoroughly. The attack exploited its internal structure to engineer a collision.

questions.workedExample:
1. Recall the three properties:
   - preimage: given a digest, find any input that hashes to it
   - second preimage: given one input, find a different input with the same hash
   - collision: find *any* two different inputs with the same hash
2. SHAttered (Google and CWI) crafted two PDFs with different content and identical SHA-1, choosing both freely.
3. That's a collision, and it was far cheaper than the generic birthday search. For a 160-bit hash a generic collision search needs about 2^80 SHA-1 computations; SHAttered needed about 2^63, roughly a hundred thousand times less work, by exploiting SHA-1's internal structure.
4. This collision result does not itself demonstrate a practical preimage attack. Practical collision attacks are already sufficient to reject SHA-1 for new signature and certificate designs.

questions.prompt: A team stores SHA-256 file fingerprints for deduplication. The database column is `CHAR(32)`, and the code writes `hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()` into it. The database silently truncates longer strings. What has actually been stored, and why does it matter?

options.text: The full digest: SHA-256 is 32 bytes, and the column holds 32 characters
options.explanation: `hexdigest()` writes each byte as two hex characters, so the full digest is 64 characters. Only half of it fits.

options.text: Half of the digest (128 bits), so the generic collision cost falls from about 2^128 to about 2^64
options.explanation: Correct. 32 hex characters carry 128 bits. Collision resistance depends on the bits you keep, so it halves in the exponent: about 2^64 work, within reach of a determined attacker who can upload chosen files.

options.text: A corrupted value that will never match, because truncation breaks SHA-256
options.explanation: Truncation is deterministic: the same file always gives the same first 32 characters, so matching still works. The problem is weaker collision resistance, not mismatches.

options.text: The full digest in compressed form, because hex is shorter than raw bytes
options.explanation: Hex is twice as long as raw bytes, not shorter: each 4 bits become one character.

questions.workedExample:
1. SHA-256 outputs 256 bits, which is 32 raw bytes. `digest()` returns those bytes; `hexdigest()` writes each byte as two hex characters, giving 64 characters.
2. A 32-character column keeps only the first 32 hex characters: 128 bits of the digest.
3. A truncated digest behaves like a shorter hash. Generic collision search costs about the square root of the output space, so 128 kept bits give roughly 2^64 work instead of 2^128.
4. For deduplication where users can upload files, an attacker who finds two colliding files could make one stand in for the other.
5. Fix: store the full value, either `CHAR(64)` for hex or 32 raw bytes in a binary column, and decide digest length from the collision resistance you need.

lessons.title: Counting collision risk with the birthday bound
lessons.summary: Collision search compares pairs, giving square-root generic work in the output space.
lessons.body:
## The birthday bound

Why does generic collision search need only about the square root of the digest space? This is the **birthday paradox**. Under a simplified model of independent, uniformly distributed birthdays over 365 days, 23 people give a 50.7% chance of a shared birthday, even though there are 365 possible days. You are not looking for a match with one particular day; you are comparing every pair, and the number of pairs grows with the square of the number of people.

The same thing happens with digests. Every new hash you compute can clash with *any* of the ones you already have, so the number of chances grows with the square of how many you have computed. Collisions therefore become likely once you have computed roughly the square root of the number of possible digests:

```formula essential
q ≈ √(N) = 2^(n/2)
where
q: the number of random hashes after which a collision becomes likely
N: the number of possible digests, 2^n
n: the digest length in bits
√: square root: √(N) is the number that multiplied by itself gives N
≈: approximately equal to; the 50 percent point is about 1.18 times this value
In words: collisions among random n-bit digests become likely after about 2^(n/2) hashes, so halving the digest length in bits gives its generic collision strength.
```

That is the practical rule: halve the digest width for its generic classical collision-strength estimate. SHA-256 gives about 128-bit collision resistance, the standard modern target. A 128-bit hash such as MD5 offered only 64 bits even before it was broken, which is within reach of a determined attacker. The same reasoning sizes random identifiers, nonces and truncated digests: in a 64-bit random ID space a clash becomes likely after a few billion items, not after 2^64.

If you need a probability rather than a rule of thumb, the standard approximation is below.

```formula reference
p ≈ 1 − e^(−q(q − 1) / (2N))
where
p: the probability that at least two of q items share a value, from 0 to 1
q: the number of items: people, or hashed messages
N: the number of equally likely values: 365 birthdays, or 2^n digests
e: Euler's number, about 2.71828, the base of natural exponentials
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the chance of a clash depends on the number of pairs, which grows with the square of q; for 23 people and 365 days it gives about 0.50, close to the exact 0.507.
```

You can watch this happen by keeping only 24 bits of SHA-256 (16,777,216 possible values) and hashing the counters 0, 1, 2, … until two collide:

```python
import hashlib, itertools

# Remember the first input for each digest.
seen = {}
for i in itertools.count():
    m = str(i).encode()
    # Only 24 bits: collisions are visible.
    h = hashlib.sha256(m).digest()[:3]
    # Equal digests from different counters.
    if h in seen:
        print(seen[h], i)
        break
    # Keep the first witness for this ID.
    seen[h] = i
```

It prints `4163 8864`: a collision after 8,865 inputs (the loop starts at zero), not after millions. Under the uniform-output model, a 24-bit collision is expected after roughly five thousand hashes, so this run is a little unlucky but unremarkable. The input sequence is fixed, so it always prints the same pair; a different sequence would collide at a different point.

## Key takeaways
- Collision search compares pairs, giving square-root generic work in the output space.
- Halve the digest length in bits for its generic collision strength; the same rule sizes random IDs and nonces.

## Further reading
- [NIST FIPS 180-4: secure hashes](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final)
- [Python hashlib API](https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html)

questions.prompt: A design document proposes identifying about 10 billion stored documents by the first 64 bits of their SHA-256 digest, with no collision handling, "because 2^64 is about 18 quintillion, so clashes will never happen". Assume the truncated digests behave like independent uniform random values. How should a reviewer respond?

options.text: Agree: with 2^64 possible IDs, 10 billion documents fill only a tiny fraction of the space
options.explanation: This compares the item count with the whole space, but collisions depend on the number of *pairs*. The birthday effect makes a clash likely once the count nears the square root of the space.

options.text: Agree, but only if documents are added slowly
options.explanation: The rate of insertion is irrelevant. What matters is how many IDs coexist, compared with the square root of the ID space.

options.text: Object: a clash becomes likely after roughly the square root of 2^64, about 4 to 5 billion IDs, so at 10 billion a collision is to be expected; use longer IDs or detect and handle collisions
options.explanation: Correct. The square root of 2^64 is 2^32, about 4.3 billion; the 50 percent point is about 5 billion. At 10 billion documents a collision is very likely.

options.text: Object: 64-bit IDs collide after about 64 documents
options.explanation: This confuses the number of bits with the number of items. Collisions become likely near 2^32 items, not 64.

questions.workedExample:
1. A collision needs *any* two of the documents to share an ID, not one particular document to hit one particular ID.
2. The number of pairs grows with the square of the document count, so clashes become likely near the square root of the ID space.
3. The square root of 2^64 is 2^32, about 4.3 billion; the 50 percent point is around 5 billion. Ten billion is beyond that, so a collision is expected, and a silent one would make two documents share an identity.
4. Options: keep more of the digest (a full 256-bit SHA-256 digest pushes the likely-collision point to about 2^128 items), or detect a clash on insert and handle it.

questions.prompt: To save space, a team truncates SHA-256 to its first 80 bits for content-addressed storage keys. An attacker can upload files of their choice. How much work does it take them to create two different files that map to the same key?

options.text: About 2^256: truncation doesn't weaken SHA-256
options.explanation: Truncation shrinks the output space. The security depends on the bits you keep, not the full internal function.

options.text: About 2^40
options.explanation: Correct as generic birthday-search work: about 2^40 hash evaluations. Actual runtime and memory or time-memory trade-offs are not specified.

options.text: About 2^80
options.explanation: That's the cost of a *preimage* (matching one given key). For a collision, where the attacker chooses both files, the birthday bound halves the exponent.

options.text: About 2^128
options.explanation: 2^128 is the collision cost of full SHA-256. With 80 bits kept, it's far lower.

questions.workedExample:
1. The attacker chooses both files, so this is a collision search, not a search for one given key.
2. Generic collision search needs about the square root of the number of possible digests, because every pair of candidates is a chance to match. Halve the bit length: 80 bits gives a 40-bit collision cost.
3. Keeping 80 bits leaves about 2^40 evaluations, roughly a trillion: a large but entirely practical computation.
4. A preimage (matching one existing file's key) would still cost about 2^80, which is why the 2^80 option is the wrong attack model here.

This is an operation count, not a measured runtime; storage and the search method matter. Choose digest length for the collision resistance you need: a full 256-bit digest targets roughly 128-bit generic collision resistance.

lessons.title: Chaining state, sponges and length extension
lessons.summary: Full-state Merkle–Damgård digests permit classic length extension; truncated variants differ.
lessons.body:
## How the common hashes are built

### Merkle–Damgård (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2)

Most older hashes split the padded message into blocks and feed them through a **compression function**, carrying a fixed-size internal state from one block to the next. A full-width digest exposes the final chaining state; truncated variants return only part of it.

```
IV -> [f] -> [f] -> [f] -> digest
       ^      ^      ^
       M1     M2     M3 (+ padding)
```

For MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512, the digest exposes the final chaining state. This does not apply equally to truncated variants such as SHA-384 and SHA-512/256. So anyone who sees the digest can carry on hashing from where it stopped. This is a **length-extension attack**. It doesn't break the hash's three properties, but it breaks naive constructions that hash a secret key followed by the message and use the result as an authentication code. The server's tag is the hash's internal state after the key, the message and the hash's own padding. An attacker who sees it can load it as their starting state, hash some extra data of their choosing, and get a valid tag for a longer message: the original message, then that padding, then the extra data. They never learn the key. The card shows this symbolically.

```formula reference
t = H(k ‖ m)
t′ = H(k ‖ m ‖ p ‖ x)
where
H: a full-state Merkle–Damgård hash such as SHA-256
k: the secret key, which the attacker never learns
m: the message the server authenticated, for example `amount=10`
t: the tag the server sends, which is also the hash's final internal state
p: the padding the hash appended after k ‖ m; it depends only on their total length, which the attacker can guess
x: extra data the attacker chooses, for example `&amount=1000`
t′: a valid tag for the longer message m ‖ p ‖ x, computed by restarting the hash from state t
‖: concatenation: joining byte strings end to end
In words: because the digest is the whole internal state, an attacker holding one valid tag can keep hashing from where the server stopped and get a valid tag for the message followed by the hash's padding and their own extra data, without knowing the key.
```

The attacker only has to guess the length of the key (trying a few values is cheap), and the forged message contains the original padding bytes in the middle, which many parsers ignore. The later HMAC unit shows how a specified keyed construction avoids it.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Continuing a till receipt from its printed total
> A shop's till prints the total so far after a list of items. Suppose the first few items are hidden, but the printed total is visible. Anyone can carry on from that total, add more items and print a valid-looking longer receipt, without ever seeing the hidden items.
>
> **How it maps:** The hidden items are the secret key, the listed items are the message, and the printed total is the digest, which for SHA-256 is the hash's whole internal state. Carrying on from the total is length extension: the attacker resumes hashing from the published state and appends their own data.
>
> **Where it stops:** A hash state is not a sum: you cannot subtract items or work backwards to the hidden ones, and the forged message must include the hash's padding bytes in the middle. A truncated or sponge-based hash prints only part of its state, like a receipt that hides part of the total, so it cannot be continued.

### Sponge (SHA-3)

**SHA-3** (Keccak, standardised in FIPS 202 in 2015) uses a different design called a **sponge construction**. It absorbs input into a large state and squeezes output from only part of it. Because the digest doesn't reveal the whole state, SHA-3 is not vulnerable to length extension. It provides a structurally different standardised alternative to SHA-2; its standardisation does not imply that SHA-2 has been broken.

## Key takeaways
- Full-state Merkle–Damgård digests permit classic length extension; truncated variants differ.
- SHA-3 hides part of its sponge state and avoids classic length extension.

## Further reading
- [NIST FIPS 180-4: secure hashes](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final)
- [NIST FIPS 202: SHA-3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/202/final)
- [RFC 2104: HMAC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104)

questions.prompt:
An API authenticates each request with a tag made by hashing a server secret followed by the request body: the secret's bytes first, then the body's, through one hash function.

For which hash functions can an attacker who sees one valid tag compute a valid tag for the body followed by the hash's padding and extra data of their choice, without the secret? Select all that apply.

options.text: SHA-256
options.explanation: Correct. SHA-256 is Merkle–Damgård and outputs its full internal state, so hashing can resume from the tag.

options.text: SHA-512
options.explanation: Correct. SHA-512 has the same Merkle–Damgård structure and full-state output, so it is equally extendable.
SHA-3 is a sponge; the output reveals only part of its state, so it can't be resumed. Not vulnerable.
This truncated SHA-512 variant hides half of its final internal state, so the attacker can't resume hashing. Not vulnerable.

options.text: MD5
options.explanation: Correct. MD5 exposes its chaining state and admits classic length extension. Duong and Rizzo described an API-signature forgery affecting Flickr in their 2009 disclosure.

questions.workedExample:
Length extension works when **the digest is the entire final internal state**:

| Hash | Structure | Extendable? |
|---|---|---|
| MD5 | MD, full state | Yes |
| SHA-256 | MD, full state | Yes |
| SHA-512 | MD, full state | Yes |
| SHA-512/256 | MD, truncated | No |
| SHA3-256 | Sponge | No |

Steps for the attacker with SHA-256:
1. Load the tag as the internal state.
2. Guess the secret's length to compute the padding.
3. Continue hashing `extra`.

The real fix is HMAC, which is safe even with SHA-256.

lessons.title: Hash families and historical collision attacks
lessons.summary: MD5 and SHA-1 lack collision resistance; choose a specified modern hash for its intended purpose.
lessons.body:
## The hash family tree

| Hash | Output | Status |
|---|---|---|
| MD5 | 128 bits | Broken collision resistance; do not use for new cryptographic designs |
| SHA-1 | 160 bits | Broken (practical collisions) |
| SHA-256 / SHA-512 | 256 / 512 | Secure, the default |
| SHA-3-256 | 256 bits | Secure |
| BLAKE2b / BLAKE2s | up to 512 / 256 bits | Configurable digest length |
| BLAKE3 | 256-bit default; extensible output | Longer output does not imply proportionally greater security |

**MD5** collisions were found in 2004 and became cheap enough to weaponise. In 2012 the Flame malware used an MD5 collision to forge a code-signing certificate that Windows Update trusted.

**SHA-1** fell in 2017, when Google and CWI Amsterdam published **SHAttered**: two different PDF files with the same SHA-1 hash. It took around 2^63 SHA-1 computations, about 6,500 CPU-years plus 110 GPU-years. Later "chosen-prefix" attacks made it cheaper still. Browser vendors phased out SHA-1-signed public TLS certificates; the 2017 collision is a historical result, not a new benchmark. In December 2022 NIST announced that SHA-1 should be phased out of its remaining uses by 31 December 2030, after which FIPS-validated cryptographic modules are not to use it (NIST IR 8547, October 2026, repeats this date). Treat any SHA-1 you find in a design today as a migration item, most urgently where collisions matter, such as signatures.

**SHA-2** (SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512 and the truncated variants SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256) is the workhorse: TLS certificates, code signing, Bitcoin, package managers. **BLAKE2** and **BLAKE3** provide modern alternatives. WireGuard specifies BLAKE2s; do not infer that each named product uses both families.

> [!tip] What to pick
> Use **SHA-256** when you need a general-purpose hash. Use SHA-512/256, SHA-3 or BLAKE2 if you want immunity to length extension. Do not choose MD5 or SHA-1 for new cryptographic designs; collision attacks do not automatically break every legacy HMAC use.

## Key takeaways
- MD5 and SHA-1 lack collision resistance; choose a specified modern hash for its intended purpose.
- A collision attack on an unkeyed hash is not automatically an HMAC forgery.

## Further reading
- [NIST FIPS 180-4: secure hashes](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final)
- [NIST FIPS 202: SHA-3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/202/final)
- [RFC 2104: HMAC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104)
- [NIST: SHA-1 retirement announcement (December 2022)](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2022/12/nist-retires-sha-1-cryptographic-algorithm)

questions.prompt: You're choosing a hash for new code. Which of these choices are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: SHA-256 for file integrity checks against a digest from a signed release manifest
options.explanation: Correct. SHA-256 is unbroken, and the digest comes from a trusted, signed source.

options.text: SHA-1 for a new code-signing system, since SHA-1 preimages are still unbroken
options.explanation: Signatures need collision resistance: an attacker who prepares two colliding files can get one signed and reuse the signature. SHA-1 collisions are practical.

options.text: BLAKE2b in keyed mode as a MAC
options.explanation: Correct. BLAKE2 has no length-extension weakness and a built-in key parameter, so keyed BLAKE2 is a sound MAC.

options.text: SHA-256 with a per-user salt for password storage
options.explanation: A salt prevents reuse of candidate-hash computations across salts, but SHA-256 is still a fast non-tunable function. Use an appropriate password-hashing scheme and deployment-specific parameters.

options.text: xxHash for detecting tampering of uploaded files
options.explanation: xxHash is a non-cryptographic hash: fast and good against accidental corruption, but an attacker can easily construct collisions.

questions.workedExample:
Match each use to the property it needs:

1. Integrity vs trusted digest: needs second-preimage resistance, plus a trusted digest. SHA-256 from a signed manifest: **sound**.
2. Code signing: needs **collision** resistance, because the attacker can influence what gets signed. SHA-1 fails: **unsound**.
3. MAC: keyed BLAKE2 is designed for this: **sound**.
4. Passwords: need a *slow* function; salted SHA-256 is still fast: **unsound**.
5. Tamper detection: needs a cryptographic hash; xxHash isn't one: **unsound**.

lessons.title: Trusted digests, Merkle paths and unambiguous inputs
lessons.summary: A digest needs a trusted comparison value to support file integrity.
lessons.body:
## What hashes are used for

- **Integrity against a trusted digest.** A download page lists the SHA-256 of a file; you hash what you received and compare. This only works if you got the digest through a channel the attacker can't change (an HTTPS page, a signed release file). If the attacker can swap both the file and the hash, a hash proves nothing.
- **Content addressing.** Git names every object by its hash. According to the Git 2.56 documentation (October 2026), new repositories still default to SHA-1, using a hardened implementation that resists the SHAttered attack; SHA-256 repositories are supported, and Git plans to make SHA-256 the default for new repositories in Git 3.0, which has no release date yet. Docker image digests, IPFS and many build caches work the same way.
